Inflation is when prices rise over time, so your money buys less than it used to.

For example, if a loaf of bread cost $2 last year and costs $2.10 this year, that's inflation of about 5%. Your dollar now covers less bread than it did before.

Some common causes:
- **Demand grows faster than supply:** people want to buy more than businesses can produce, so sellers raise prices.
- **Costs go up:** if wages, materials, or energy get more expensive, businesses pass those costs on to customers.
- **More money in circulation:** when there's more money chasing the same goods, each unit of money is worth a little less.

A small amount of inflation (around 2% a year, in many countries) is considered normal and even healthy, since it encourages spending and investing. Very high inflation is harmful because it erodes savings and makes planning difficult.

Inflation is when prices for everyday things, like groceries, rent, and gas, go up over time. As a result, each dollar you have buys a little less than it did before.

For example, if a coffee cost $3 last year and costs $3.15 this year, that's about 5% inflation. Your money didn't shrink, but it now covers less stuff.

Inflation happens for a few main reasons:
- **Demand is higher than supply:** lots of people want to buy things, but there isn't enough to go around, so sellers raise prices.
- **Costs go up:** if it becomes more expensive to make or transport things, companies often pass those costs on to customers.
- **More money in circulation:** when there's more money floating around, each dollar tends to be worth less.

A little inflation is normal and considered healthy for an economy. Too much, though, makes life harder because your paycheck may not keep up with rising prices.

Inflation is when prices for things you buy go up over time, so your money buys less than it used to.

For example, if a cup of coffee cost $2 last year and costs $2.10 this year, that's inflation. Your dollar now covers a little less coffee than it did before.

A small amount of inflation (around 2% a year) is normal and considered healthy, since it encourages people to spend and invest rather than hoard cash. But when inflation rises quickly, everyday life gets more expensive fast, and savings lose value if they aren't growing as fast as prices.

Common causes include:
- **Demand rising faster than supply**, like lots of people wanting to buy the same things.
- **Production costs rising**, like higher wages or fuel prices passed on to customers.
- **Money being printed or made more available**, which can make each unit of money worth less.
